paragraphs: I flatter myself that my last number clearly showed that the particular States, under the proposed Constitution, would have COEQUAL authority with the Union in the matter of revenue, except as to duties on imports. Since this leaves open to the States by far the greatest part of the community's resources, there can be no pretext for asserting that they would lack means as abundant as could be desired to supply their own wants, independent of all outside control. That the field is wide enough will appear more fully when we come to the small share of the public expenses that will fall to the State governments to provide.

To argue from abstract principles that this coordinate authority cannot exist is to set supposition and theory against fact and reality. Such reasoning may be proper for showing that a thing OUGHT NOT TO EXIST, but it must be wholly rejected when it is used to prove that a thing does not exist, against the evidence of the fact itself. It is well known that in the Roman republic the legislative authority, in the last resort, resided for ages in two different political bodies. They were not branches of the same legislature but distinct and independent legislatures, and in each an opposite interest prevailed: in one the patrician, in the other the plebeian. Many arguments might have been offered to prove the unfitness of two such seemingly contradictory authorities, each having power to ANNUL or REPEAL the acts of the other. But a man who attempted at Rome to disprove their existence would have been regarded as frantic. It will be readily understood that I am alluding to the COMITIA CENTURIATA and the COMITIA TRIBUTA. The former, in which the people voted by centuries, was so arranged as to give superiority to the patrician interest; in the latter, in which numbers prevailed, the plebeian interest had complete predominance. And yet these two legislatures coexisted for ages, and the Roman republic reached the utmost height of human greatness.

In the case now under consideration, there is no such contradiction as appears in the example cited; there is no power on either side to annul the acts of the other. And in practice there is little reason to fear any problem. In a short time the wants of the States will naturally reduce themselves WITHIN A VERY NARROW COMPASS, and in the meantime the United States will in all probability find it convenient to abstain wholly from those objects to which the particular States would be inclined to turn.

To form a more precise judgment of the true merits of this question, it will be well to look at the proportion between the objects that will require a federal provision of revenue and those that will require a State provision. We shall discover that the former are altogether unlimited and that the latter are confined within very moderate bounds. In pursuing this inquiry we must bear in mind that we are not to confine our view to the present period, but are to look forward to remote futurity. Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed on a calculation of existing necessities, but on a combination of these with the probable necessities of ages, according to the natural and tried course of human affairs. Nothing, therefore, can be more fallacious than to infer from an estimate of its immediate necessities the extent of any power that is proper to be lodged in the national government. There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they may happen; and since these are illimitable in their nature, it is impossible to limit that capacity safely. It is true, perhaps, that a computation might be made with sufficient accuracy for the purpose of the quantity of revenue required to discharge the existing engagements of the Union and to maintain those establishments which would suffice in time of peace for some time to come. But would it be wise, or would it not rather be the extreme of folly, to stop at this point, and to leave the government entrusted with the care of the national defense in a state of absolute incapacity to provide for the protection of the community against future invasions of the public peace, by foreign war or domestic convulsions? If, on the contrary, we ought to go beyond this point, where can we stop short of an indefinite power of providing for emergencies as they may arise? It is easy to assert, in general terms, that a rational judgment can be formed of a proper provision against probable dangers. But we may safely challenge those who make the assertion to bring forward their data, and may affirm that those data would be found as vague and uncertain as any that could be produced to establish the probable duration of the world. Observations confined to the mere prospect of internal attacks can deserve no weight, though even these admit of no satisfactory calculation. And if we mean to be a commercial people, it must be part of our policy to be able one day to defend that commerce. The support of a navy and of naval wars would involve contingencies that must baffle all the efforts of political arithmetic.

Suppose we admit that we ought to try the novel and absurd experiment in politics of tying the hands of government against offensive war founded on reasons of state. Certainly we ought not to disable it from guarding the community against the ambition or enmity of other nations. A cloud has been hanging over the European world for some time. If it should break into a storm, who can assure us that in its progress part of its fury would not be spent upon us? No reasonable man would hastily pronounce that we are entirely out of its reach. Or if the combustible materials that now seem to be gathering should disperse without coming to maturity, or if a flame should be kindled without extending to us, what security can we have that our tranquillity will long remain undisturbed from some other cause or some other quarter? Let us remember that peace or war will not always be left to our choice; that however moderate or unambitious we may be, we cannot count on the moderation of others, or hope to extinguish their ambition. Who could have imagined, at the conclusion of the last war, that France and Britain, wearied and exhausted as they both were, would so soon look on each other with so hostile an aspect? To judge from the history of mankind, we shall be compelled to conclude that the fiery and destructive passions of war reign in the human breast with much more powerful sway than the mild and beneficent feelings of peace, and that to model our political systems on speculations of lasting tranquillity is to calculate on the weaker springs of the human character.

What are the chief sources of expense in every government? What has caused that enormous accumulation of debts with which several of the European nations are oppressed? The answer plainly is: wars and rebellions, and the support of those institutions which are necessary to guard the body politic against these two most mortal diseases of society. The expenses of institutions that relate to the mere domestic police of a state, to the support of its legislative, executive and judicial departments with their different appendages, and to the encouragement of agriculture and manufactures (which will comprehend almost all the objects of state expenditure), are insignificant in comparison with those that relate to the national defense.

In the kingdom of Great Britain, where all the ostentatious apparatus of monarchy must be provided for, not above a fifteenth part of the nation's annual income is appropriated to the class of expenses last mentioned. The other fourteen fifteenths are absorbed in paying the interest on debts contracted to carry on the wars in which that country has been engaged, and in maintaining fleets and armies. On the one hand, it may be observed that the expenses of pursuing the ambitious enterprises and vainglorious projects of a monarchy are not a proper standard by which to judge those which might be necessary in a republic. On the other hand, it ought to be remarked that there should be an equally great disproportion between the profusion and extravagance of a wealthy kingdom in its domestic administration and the frugality and economy which in that respect become the modest simplicity of republican government. If we balance a proper deduction from one side against that which it is supposed ought to be made from the other, the proportion may still be considered to hold good.

But let us look at the large debt we ourselves contracted in a single war, and let us calculate on only a common share of the events that disturb the peace of nations. We shall instantly perceive, without the aid of any elaborate illustration, that there must always be an immense disproportion between the objects of federal and of State expenditures. It is true that several of the States, separately, are burdened with considerable debts, which are an outgrowth of the recent war. But this cannot happen again if the proposed system is adopted; and when these debts are discharged, the only call for revenue of any consequence that the State governments will continue to experience will be for the mere support of their respective civil lists. If we add all contingencies to this, the total amount in every State ought to fall considerably short of two hundred thousand pounds.

In framing a government for posterity as well as for ourselves, we ought, in those provisions that are designed to be permanent, to calculate not on temporary but on permanent causes of expense. If this principle is just, our attention would be directed to providing the State governments with an annual sum of about two hundred thousand pounds, while the necessities of the Union could be susceptible of no limits, even in imagination. In this view of the subject, by what logic can it be maintained that the local governments ought to command, in perpetuity, an EXCLUSIVE source of revenue for any sum beyond two hundred thousand pounds? To extend their power further, in EXCLUSION of the authority of the Union, would be to take the resources of the community out of the hands that needed them for the public welfare, in order to put them into other hands that could have no just or proper occasion for them.

Suppose, then, that the Convention had been inclined to proceed on the principle of dividing the objects of revenue between the Union and its members in PROPORTION to their comparative necessities. What particular fund could have been selected for the use of the States that would not have been either too much or too little: too little for their present wants, too much for their future wants? As to the line of separation between external and internal taxes, this would leave to the States, by a rough computation, the command of two thirds of the community's resources to pay from a tenth to a twentieth part of its expenses, and would leave to the Union one third of the community's resources to pay from nine tenths to nineteen twentieths of its expenses. If we abandon this boundary and content ourselves with leaving to the States an exclusive power of taxing houses and lands, there would still be a great disproportion between the MEANS and the END: the possession of one third of the community's resources to supply, at most, one tenth of its wants. If any fund could have been selected and appropriated that was equal to the object and no greater, it would have been inadequate to discharge the existing debts of the particular States, and would have left them dependent on the Union for a provision for this purpose.

The preceding train of observations will justify the position laid down elsewhere, that "A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union." Any separation of the objects of revenue that could have been hit upon would have amounted to a sacrifice of the great INTERESTS of the Union to the POWER of the individual States. The Convention thought the concurrent jurisdiction preferable to that subordination; and it is evident that it has at least the merit of reconciling an indefinite constitutional power of taxation in the federal government with an adequate and independent power in the States to provide for their own necessities. There remain a few other lights in which this important subject of taxation will claim further consideration.
